blocks.title: Galvanic (voltaic) cell
blocks.text: A galvanic cell is a cell in which the conversion of chemical energy into electrical energy takes place spontaneously in an exothermic redox process, with oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode. It is designed to take advantage of the spontaneous transfer of electrons; a galvanic cell is also known as a voltaic cell, for example the Daniell cell and the dry cell.

To measure the electrode potential of the half-equation Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s), a pure copper rod is placed in a solution of Cu2+(aq) ions such as copper(II) sulfate; this Cu2+/Cu system is a half-cell, made under standard conditions: Cu2+ at 1.00 mol dm-3, 25 degrees C (298 K) and a pure copper rod. Connecting two half-cells makes an electrochemical cell whose voltage can be measured. Figure 10.7 shows a Cu2+/Cu half-cell connected to a Zn2+/Zn half-cell (Zn2+ + 2e- giving Zn, -0.76 V).

The half-cells are connected by wires joining the metal rods to a high-resistance voltmeter, through which the electrons flow round the external circuit from the metal with the more negative (less positive) electrode potential to the metal with the less negative (more positive) one; and by a salt bridge, which completes the electrical circuit by allowing the movement of ions between the two half-cells so that ionic balance is maintained, but does not allow the movement of electrons. A salt bridge can be a strip of filter paper (or other inert porous material) soaked in saturated potassium nitrate solution.

blocks.alt: Left: two beakers, zinc in zinc sulfate and copper in copper sulfate, joined by an orange salt bridge and by wires through a voltmeter reading +1.10 V, with a green arrow showing electron flow from zinc to copper and the half-equations below. Top right: the standard cell potential rule with the Cu/Zn, Ag/Zn and Cu/Fe examples. Bottom right: feasibility from E standard with the magnesium-silver, iron-silver and aluminium-silver cases and the rule about the stronger oxidising and reducing agents.
blocks.caption: The Zn-Cu galvanic cell, standard cell potentials, direction of electron flow and feasibility (original diagram after Figures 10.7 to 10.10 and topics 10.15 to 10.17.3 and 10.21).
blocks.long_description: Zinc, with the more negative electrode potential, is the anode and dissolves as zinc ions; the electrons it releases travel through the wire to the copper cathode, where copper ions are reduced and plate out, and the salt bridge lets ions move so that neither solution builds up charge. The cell voltage is the difference between the two standard potentials, 1.10 V for copper and zinc, 1.56 V for silver and zinc. Any pair of half-equations can be tested the same way: if the more positive half-cell is written as the reduction and the more negative as the oxidation the cell potential is positive and the reaction is feasible, which is why magnesium reduces silver ions but silver cannot reduce magnesium or aluminium ions.

blocks.text: The half-equations are Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s), E standard = +0.34 V, and Zn2+(aq) + 2e- giving Zn(s), E standard = -0.76 V. The relative values show that Zn2+ ions are more difficult to reduce than Cu2+ ions, and the voltage generated by the cell is +1.10 V: E cell = E(reduction) - E(oxidation) = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V. In the Cu-Zn galvanic cell zinc is the anode and the copper ions in solution the cathode: at the anode zinc is oxidised, Zn(s) giving Zn2+(aq) + 2e-; the electrons travel through the external circuit to the cathode, where copper ions are reduced, Cu2+(aq) + 2e- giving Cu(s); the overall cell reaction is Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) giving Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s). The chemical energy of the redox reaction is converted into electrical energy that can do work.
What are the functions and advantages of the salt bridge, and what happens to the voltage if it is removed?
